slides.title: The interface must fit the animal’s vision and body
body: The joystick apparatus separated the monitor from the pig with a transparent window. A rounded knob supported snout contact rather than the hand grip used by primates. The device therefore translated an existing movement repertoire into a computer input.

The pigs were **hyperopic**, meaning that their eyes focused more readily on distant than nearby objects. Refraction measurements guided placement of the monitor approximately 45 cm from their eyes. Visual access was an experimentally adjusted property of the apparatus.
Cursor movement occurred at 8 cm/s on a 33 cm monitor. These dimensions determined how far a pig had to push the joystick and how quickly the visible outcome changed during a response.

slides.title: Shaping builds the joystick response gradually
body: **Shaping** reinforces successive approximations to a desired behavior. The pigs first received food for approaching a mock joystick, then for manipulating it with their snouts. A spring-mounted knob allowed practice before cursor control was introduced.

After this preparation, reinforcement followed orientation toward the monitor. The instruction to watch the screen was paired with joystick manipulation, linking visual attention and motor action within the same trained sequence.

The mock-joystick stage lasted two weeks. Food delivery, verbal feedback and tactile contact accompanied successful responding during subsequent testing. The trained action was therefore supported by an explicit reinforcement history, including social responses from the handler.

slides.title: Fewer target walls require more selective movement
body: The **SIDE task** began with a cursor in the middle of a screen bordered by four target walls. Any completed outward movement could reach a wall. Removing walls progressively required selection of the direction that still contained a rewarded target.

With one wall present, only one of the four main initial directions was correct. Target location varied among the top, bottom, left and right of the screen, preventing one repeated direction from solving every trial.

The program adjusted difficulty according to response speed. Successful responding led to fewer or shorter walls; slower responding restored easier conditions. The task thus changed the precision required while retaining the same joystick-to-cursor mapping.

slides.title: Initial cursor direction distinguishes target selection
body: Reaching some screen border after repeated movements is different from directing the cursor correctly on the first attempt. Croney and Boysen scored the first cursor movement to separate target selection from eventual contact after an extended search.

On the one-wall task, the Yorkshire pigs reached the correct target initially more often than random directional choices would predict. They also performed above random expectation when only two walls remained available.

Performance varied with target position. Vertical movements were generally easier for the Yorkshire pigs than horizontal movements. The position dependence linked the measured outcome to the physical demands of joystick manipulation as well as to learned visual selection.

slides.title: Individual pigs acquire different control strategies
body: The micro pigs differed markedly in one-wall performance. Ivory acquired effective responding across all target positions, whereas Ebony's strongest responding occurred toward selected locations. A single species-level description would conceal these distinct control patterns.

The micro pigs generally performed better in the horizontal plane, unlike the vertical advantage of the Yorkshire pigs. The animals therefore did not share one universal directional bias imposed by the task.

The training procedure was revised when easy trials dominated the micro pigs' sessions. Requiring exposure to two-wall and one-wall trials provided repeated experience with directional selection. Access to the more demanding contingencies was itself part of learning the task.

slides.title: Motor constraints can limit apparently cognitive tasks
body: A pig moving a joystick must orient the head, maintain visual access and apply force to a knob with its snout. These movements are mechanically different from a primate manipulating a joystick with its fingers.

The Yorkshire pigs eventually became too large for the apparatus. Growth changed the body's fit to the testing environment without changing the abstract rule that cursor contact produced a reward. The animals' ability to participate depended on the physical interface.

Croney and Boysen proposed touchscreen testing as an alternative for pigs. Direct contact with a displayed target can reduce the indirect movement demands of joystick control while retaining computerized stimulus presentation and response recording.

slides.title: Touchscreens translate nose contact into recorded choices
body: Ao and colleagues built a touchscreen system for pigs in which a nose press registered a response to a displayed button. A computer logged each response and controlled auditory feedback and food delivery.

The completed apparatus used an industrial resistive screen in a weighted rack. **Resistive sensing** detected pressure on the screen, allowing contact by the pig's snout to operate the device. The rack could be adjusted for animals of different heights.

Food was delivered away from the screen through a separately controlled dispenser. Separating the response surface from food reduced rooting toward the monitor while preserving the relationship between a successful screen response and its consequence.

figure.caption: Ao et al. (2022), Fig. 1. Device components and completed pig touchscreen.

refs: Ao W, Grace M, Floyd CL, Vonder Haar C (2022). A Touchscreen Device for Behavioral Testing in Pigs. Biomedicines 10:2612. https://doi.org/10.3390/biomedicines10102612

Immediate tones also distinguished an accepted contact from an unregistered movement.

slides.title: A nose swipe changes where software registers a choice
body: Pigs often pressed a target and then swiped upward at a slight diagonal. When software registered the release of contact, the recorded response could occur above the button that the pig initially touched.

Ao and colleagues changed the buttons to respond on initial touch. This altered the event that counted as a choice while leaving the animal's contact movement largely intact. A software convention could otherwise turn an accurate initial press into an apparent error.

Tones identified a registered response and the beginning of a trial. Auditory feedback supplied an immediate consequence when the screen itself provided little tactile confirmation that the computer had accepted the movement.

slides.title: Delayed rewards change touchscreen choice
body: **Delay discounting** is a reduction in the value assigned to a reward when obtaining it requires waiting. The pigs chose between a button delivering one pellet and a button delivering four pellets.

When both outcomes were immediate, training established preference for the larger reward. The experiment then introduced delays before the four-pellet outcome while leaving the smaller outcome available sooner. Reward magnitude and waiting time were manipulated separately.

Pigs rapidly avoided delayed reinforcement. Adjustments to button locations and delay schedules were used during device testing, and later choice remained sensitive to the introduced delay. The touchscreen made the temporal cost of an action part of its learned consequence.

slides.title: Correction trials support color discrimination
body: In the initial color task, choosing the yellow button produced food while the blue button did not. The locations of the buttons varied, so successful responding required using color rather than always touching the same side.

Accuracy was initially low. A **correction trial** repeated an incorrectly answered problem while making the incorrect option inactive. After this change, accurate color selection increased rapidly over one or two sessions.

The subsequent conditional task required the pig to select the color matching a preceding central stimulus. Accuracy declined when this additional relation was introduced. Learning one rewarded color was therefore behaviorally different from selecting a color according to a changing sample.

slides.title: Response demands shape participation as well as accuracy
body: The touchscreen pigs explored their surroundings during testing, sometimes leaving the device during a trial. A tone signaling trial onset helped reorient them toward the screen. The testing room contained competing opportunities for action.

Increasing the required number of presses made the color task more demanding. The added response requirement did not restore accurate conditional matching, and withholding expected food could interrupt re-engagement with the screen.

Device durability also changed participation. The first screen broke during repeated testing, whereas the revised industrial version remained intact. Recorded performance emerged from an interaction among learned task rules, response demands, reinforcement delivery and an apparatus able to withstand the animal's movements.

slides.title: Portable touchscreens bring tasks into social enclosures
body: Martin and colleagues developed **Apex**, a battery-powered touchscreen mounted on the mesh of a primate enclosure. An animal-facing screen presented stimuli, while a separate interface allowed the experimenter to control the task.

The device included food delivery, sound and colored light feedback. Responses could be tested where the macaques already lived, avoiding a requirement to transport each animal into a separate testing chamber for every session.

ApeTouch software provided training, preference and discrimination tasks through the same apparatus. The physical device remained stable while the stimulus arrangement and response rule changed. Computerized testing thus separated the animal's access to an interface from the particular problem presented on it.

slides.title: Smaller dots train more precise screen contact
body: The first Apex training task presented one black dot at a random screen location. Touching it removed the dot and produced a chime, light feedback and a food pellet. Each trial linked a specific visual target to a direct hand movement.
The dot initially occupied much of the screen. Its diameter was reduced from 550 to 100 pixels over training, progressively increasing the precision required to contact the stimulus.

Randomized target position made the macaques follow the dot across the screen rather than repeat a single movement. The consequence remained consistent as target size changed, allowing the same basic response to become spatially more selective.

slides.title: Touching two targets introduces a response sequence
body: The Two Dot task presented two targets simultaneously. Touching either target removed it, but food arrived only after both had been contacted. A first successful movement therefore left a second required movement unfinished.

The Two Number Dot task added numerals to the same basic arrangement. Touching the dot labeled 1 before the dot labeled 2 produced reinforcement; beginning with 2 produced an error signal and no food.

The rule required a learned order of contact rather than simply two screen touches. Random target positions prevented a fixed spatial sequence from solving the task, linking the order of movements to the visible numerals.

slides.title: Social rank changes who gets access to the interface
body: The touchscreen was available to macaques living in groups. In the rhesus and Japanese groups, a dominant individual monopolized the device. In the Tibetan and bonnet groups, several individuals commonly shared access.

A group-level record of screen responses therefore did not mean that all members had equal experience. Competition for the device changed who could practice the visual and motor contingencies during the testing period.

Usage generally increased across training. Access patterns were recorded alongside trial completion, allowing engagement with the task to be separated from the distribution of opportunities within the social group. An enclosure-based interface became part of the group's social environment.

slides.title: Practice and forced trials change sequencing performance
body: Japanese and bonnet macaques acquired above-random performance on the Two Number Dot task and maintained it during subsequent testing. The rhesus and Tibetan groups did not reach that level within the study period.

Forced trials were excluded when performance on the two-choice task was evaluated. This retained the distinction between producing a required movement when no alternative was available and selecting the correct first movement when both numbered targets appeared.

slides.title: Macaques choose which touchscreen task to perform
body: Calapai and colleagues offered rhesus macaques a **multiple-choice interface** with three task buttons. An animal could select a stationary-target task, a moving-target task or picture viewing at the start of a trial.

The reaching tasks delivered diluted juice after a correct touch. Picture viewing delivered neither fluid reward nor an additional response requirement. The animals could therefore choose between different forms of engagement with the same screen.

The interface operated in their living environment without social separation or fluid restriction for this study. Each button selection opened a particular set of sensory and response consequences, making task selection itself an observable behavior.

slides.title: Task preferences persist across button locations
body: A monkey that repeatedly touches one side of a screen may appear to prefer a task simply because its button is located there. The multiple-choice study changed button arrangements to separate spatial bias from task selection.

Most animals with consistent task preferences favored the stationary-target task; others favored the moving-target task. The preference analysis considered button position as well as repeated selections across time and sessions.

The distinction between preferred task and preferred location depended on presenting the same task through different spatial arrangements. The animal's choices could then be related to task consequences rather than attributed automatically to the shape or side of a button.

slides.title: Rats move a vehicle by completing an electrical circuit
body: Crawford and colleagues built a **rodent-operated vehicle**, or ROV, with a transparent driver compartment on a motorized chassis. A rat standing on an aluminum floor plate could move the vehicle by touching copper bars.

Contact between the floor plate and a bar completed an electrical circuit through the animal's body. The resulting signal activated the controller and motors. Releasing the bar stopped movement, linking a discrete contact action to whole-body transport.

The controller translated contact into vehicle motion rather than requiring walking to move toward the destination. Voluntary entry into the compartment preceded the control action, so approaching the device and operating it were separable components of the trained behavior.

slides.title: Driving is shaped from entering to reaching a goal
body: Before training, a container resembling the vehicle compartment was placed in the rats' home cages. Food rewards were also introduced in advance. **Habituation**, a reduction in responding to a repeatedly encountered stimulus, reduced novelty before driving contingencies were imposed.

Training reinforced vehicle entry, contact with the bars and increasingly long forward movements. The goal end of the arena carried a checkerboard marker, providing a visible destination for the driving response.

Food was available only through the vehicle task. Increasing the distance required before delivery progressively extended the same learned contact response into movement toward a remote goal, rather than reinforcing bar contact regardless of where the vehicle traveled.

slides.title: Enriched housing changes experience before driving
body: The rat-driving experiment compared animals housed in a multilevel enriched enclosure with animals in standard cages. The enriched enclosure included natural and artificial objects that changed weekly, providing varied opportunities for movement and exploration.

Housing exposure preceded driving training by approximately four months. The comparison therefore tested how an extended history of environmental interaction related to acquiring a new machine-control task.

The enriched rats acquired robust driving responses more readily than the standard-housed rats. Environmental experience altered subsequent engagement with a novel interface, even though the vehicle's contact-to-motion rule was the same for both housing conditions.

slides.title: Approaching the vehicle and driving improve separately
body: Successful driving contained several stages: entering the vehicle, touching its controls and completing forward movement to the reward location. The investigators recorded progress through these stages rather than treating every unsuccessful trial as the same event.

Enriched-housed animals reached the entry and control criteria more readily. They also more effectively acquired repeated complete drives. The acquisition record linked participation with the eventual coordinated action sequence.

The vehicle was not simply a passive transport cage. The rat had to approach it, activate its contact controls and maintain the response while the surrounding scene changed. Improvements in this sequence depended on acquiring both willingness to engage and effective control.

slides.title: Extinction separates practiced actions from current food
body: **Extinction** is a change in behavior when an outcome that previously followed a response is withheld. After driving training, the rats encountered the vehicle in trials without an opportunity to obtain the usual food reward.

A previously reinforced interface can continue to recruit behavior after its immediate food consequence changes. The extinction comparison therefore added a measure of persistence to the acquisition record, rather than assuming that repeated vehicle entry was entirely determined by food available on that trial.

slides.title: Pigeons steer a virtual avatar with directional pecks
body: Rodrigues and colleagues trained pigeons to navigate a **virtual avatar**, a screen object whose movements were controlled by the animal. The avatar resembled Pacman, and reaching a banana icon produced food access rather than a real banana.

Pecking the avatar exposed directional guides around it. A peck on a guide moved the avatar 120 pixels in that direction. The bird's beak contacted the screen locally while the controlled object moved through a larger virtual arena.

Pecking the banana itself had no effect. Reinforcement depended on moving the avatar to the goal, separating attraction to the visible target from learning the action that changed the avatar's position.

slides.title: Training builds navigation from a two-response chain
body: The pigeons first learned to peck the avatar at fixed and then changing screen positions. Training subsequently introduced one directional guide, so an avatar peck followed by a guide peck became a **response chain**, a sequence with successive action requirements.

Presenting several guides made movement direction a choice. Initially, the banana was one step away; later it required two steps, including diagonal arrangements that demanded two different directional selections.

Trials with unrestricted steps allowed birds to continue navigating after an inefficient choice. Training thus changed from producing a required response to selecting successive movements toward a goal whose position varied, while food followed completion of the route.

slides.title: Virtual barriers require detours rather than direct pursuit
body: A barrier occupied a cell within the pigeons' virtual arena and blocked avatar movement through that location. Direct movement toward a visible banana could therefore fail to provide a traversable route to it.

Training introduced one barrier and then two barriers. The avatar initially began to the left of the obstacle and the banana to the right; reversing these positions tested navigation with a changed start-to-goal arrangement.

The birds that progressed learned to move around the barriers. Final navigation quizzes varied the avatar and banana locations across the arena, requiring routes of two to nine steps at minimum. A successful movement sequence depended on both goal location and the space available around the obstacle.

slides.title: Neural activity can control reaching on a screen
body: Carmena and colleagues trained macaques to move a cursor toward a target and to control a virtual grip. During initial training, the animal manipulated a handheld pole while electrodes recorded activity from populations of neurons in the cortex, the brain’s outer gray matter. The recordings captured action potentials, the brief electrical spikes generated by neurons.
A **brain–machine interface** used recorded activity to predict movement parameters. The controller could then move the cursor using those predictions rather than the pole's current displacement.

The animal received continuous visual feedback about cursor position and grip. Switching from pole control to neural control changed the source of the computer command while preserving the visible goal, allowing the same practiced task to be performed through a different output pathway.

slides.title: A decoder links population firing to motor parameters
body: A **decoder** is a model translating recorded neural activity into an output command. In Carmena's preparation, models predicted hand position, velocity and gripping force from the activity of cortical neuronal ensembles.

During an initial pole-control period, recorded activity was paired with measured movement. Model coefficients were then fixed before the animal controlled the cursor through the neural interface. Improvement could occur while the activity-to-command transformation remained stable.

The same population carried information about several movement parameters. Combining neuronal activity supplied a usable control signal for reaching and grip rather than assigning one recorded neuron to a single complete movement or treating all cortical activity as interchangeable.

slides.title: Brain control continues without arm movement
body: The macaques initially moved their arms during brain control, continuing the behavior associated with pole manipulation. With experience, they produced periods of effective cursor control while their arms remained still.

**Electromyography**, or EMG, records electrical activity associated with muscle activation. Surface EMG from arm muscles lost its movement-linked modulation during these periods, while the neural decoder continued moving the cursor.

Removing the pole further separated neural control from the original mechanical action. The task could be completed through cortical activity and visual feedback without the arm providing the immediate movement signal used during initial training.

slides.title: Robot dynamics change the animal’s control problem
body: A real robot arm and gripper were introduced into the closed control loop. Robot position determined the displayed cursor location, and gripper force determined cursor size. The visual feedback now represented a physical actuator's response.
The robot introduced a 60–90 ms delay between decoder output and movement. Initial performance declined when these dynamics entered the loop, even though the target-selection rule remained unchanged.

Practice restored performance over approximately seven training sessions. The animal adjusted to consequences imposed by the actuator, linking skill acquisition to the timing and dynamics of the controlled device as well as to the neural decoder's immediate output.

slides.title: Directional tuning changes across control modes
body: **Directional tuning** is a relationship between a neuron's firing and the direction of movement. Carmena and colleagues compared this relationship during pole control, brain control with arm movement and brain control without arm movement.

Neuronal firing patterns changed when control shifted between these conditions. The cortical population's activity was therefore not a fixed copy of the same arm movement replayed unchanged through every interface.

The recorded tuning patterns linked the visual task to the active control mode. Brain control without arm movement required neuronal activity appropriate for producing cursor trajectories through the decoder, connecting a learned artificial output relationship with changes in population firing.

slides.title: Practice reorganizes the neural population response
body: Repeated brain-control sessions improved the animal's performance while the relationship between neural activity and direction also changed. Population activity became organized around the directions relevant to the controlled cursor.

Individual neurons contributed differently across practice. These shifts occurred within an ensemble whose output was used by the fixed movement decoder, so changing neuronal patterns altered the commands reaching the device.

The result connected **neural plasticity**, a change in neural function with experience, to acquisition of an interface skill. Behavioral improvement and population reorganization accompanied learning to control an external output through activity rather than through the previously trained arm movement.

slides.title: Reaching and gripping require coordinated neural outputs
body: The combined reach-and-grasp task required moving the cursor to a target and then developing the instructed grip. Cursor position represented reaching, while cursor size conveyed gripping force. Successful performance coordinated these distinct output dimensions.

Carmena and colleagues extracted position and grip information from the same recorded neuronal ensemble. Neural activity around grip onset remained structured during brain control, linking the population response to the task's successive behavioral demands.

Across joystick, touchscreen, vehicle and neural interfaces, reinforcement followed a specific relationship between action and feedback. Changing the controlled output altered the movements or neural patterns needed for success, while repeated practice established a usable mapping to the visible goal.

items.text: Animals acquire relationships between their actions, remote visual consequences and reinforcement across joystick, touchscreen and vehicle interfaces.
Vision, body size, contact movements and social access determine which actions an interface records and which animals can practice.
Target position, size, movement and response order distinguish spatial selection, precision, timing and sequence learning.
Enriched housing supported rat-driving acquisition and persistence; reinforcement timing changed touchscreen choices.
Pigeons transferred trained portal use to new puzzles; a previously rewarded operation could also attract repeated actions when direct navigation was more effective.
Macaques learned cursor and grip control from cortical populations without arm movement; practice changed population tuning and compensation for robot dynamics.
